title: The most common misconceptions about nuclear war | Jeffrey Lewis (2022)
summary: Arms-control expert Jeffrey Lewis (2022) on why deterrence is shakier than game theory suggests, US nuclear doctrine, escalation pathways and the arms race with Russia and China.

assertions.quote: because the president got up on the wrong side of the bed, because the information is wrong — things get out of control.

verdicts.note: Documented false alarms such as 1983 and 1995 show accidental or mistaken launch is possible, though safeguards have held so far.

assertions.quote: deterrence will eventually fail if you do it long enough, and it will fail catastrophically

verdicts.note: It follows if a non-zero annual risk persists, but that risk can be lowered and the claim cannot be tested over its horizon.

The model and Hellman's estimate put deterrence failure on the order of 1 percent a year, implying high cumulative odds over a long horizon, but the authors stress wide uncertainty and that ranges matter more than point values.

Clauset: under stationarity, the median wait for a billion-death war, plausible only with wide nuclear use, is about 1,339 years (5-95%: 383-11,489); the author calls this sobering but its plausibility likely unknowable.

assertions.quote: My answer is, it’s 1 in 100, 1 in 1,000. It’s a small number.

verdicts.note: Expert and forecaster estimates of annual great-power nuclear war risk run from a fraction of a percent to about one percent, which compounds over decades.

Metaculus forecasters put a deliberate nuclear detonation as an act of war at 34% between 2020 and 2050: a small yearly risk (about 1.4% a year) that adds up, though the question counts any belligerent, not only great powers.
Expert surveys since 1997 put annualized nuclear-war or nuclear-catastrophe risks between about 0.05% and 2.2% a year: small each year but cumulative, e.g. 29% for nuclear use in combat by 2047.

A fault-tree model estimates the annual probability of inadvertent US-Russia nuclear war at a mean of 0.02 (median 0.009, 90 percent range 0.0002-0.07), consistent with Hellman's roughly 1 percent a year, a small yearly risk that compounds over decades.

Clauset: a constant annual hazard of very large interstate war adds up to about 43% for a WWII-sized war per century, which is the small-but-cumulative logic applied to large wars rather than nuclear war specifically.

Braumoeller: at 50 wars per century there is about a 13% chance of a war killing over 1% of humanity in the next 100 years; the risk is cumulative, but the estimate covers all large wars, not nuclear war.

assertions.quote: I think deterrence is probably less effective than people believe. The examples I always give are Argentina invaded the Falklands.

verdicts.note: The Falklands, the 1973 war, the 1969 Sino-Soviet clashes and Kargil show nuclear-armed states attacked on a limited scale.

assertions.quote: The whole idea of mutual assured destruction is you accept the possibility of reciprocal deterrence. And our policy is not to do that.

verdicts.note: Declassified US guidance since Carter and Reagan speaks of prevailing and limiting damage, though leaders also say a nuclear war cannot be won.

RAND says MAD was a condition both superpowers hoped to escape and the US built assured-retaliation and countervailing strategies that went beyond it, which fits the claim for the Cold War but is about denying enemy aims rather than prevailing in a nuclear war.

assertions.quote: if they see submarine-launched ballistic missiles coming at Russia, even if it’s only one, they’re going to assume that there are more

verdicts.note: War games and stated Russian doctrine suggest escalation control is fragile, though no nuclear exchange has tested it.
A deliberate nuclear detonation would multiply FRI participants' forecast of a 10-million-death catastrophe 4x (experts) to 6.7x (superforecasters): a large added risk of escalation.

RAND warns that once Russia decided to use nuclear weapons it might be relatively unrestrained in number and type, seeing little difference in cost between small and large use; it does not model a full exchange with NATO.

assertions.quote: the Russians and the Chinese are investing really heavily in medium- and intermediate-range missiles that can do both nuclear and conventional missions.

verdicts.note: Entanglement of conventional and nuclear systems is a widely recognised escalation pathway in Carnegie and RAND studies.

DoD says China's long-range precision strike has 'blurred the boundaries between strategic, operational, and tactical levels of war' and that reliance on strategic (likely nuclear) deterrence shows comfort with conventional escalation; it is about China and not dual-capable missiles in general.
US intelligence says Russia's nuclear threats and combat use of dual-capable IRBMs in Ukraine raise the specter of a regional war becoming an existential threat to the US.

In the May 2025 India-Pakistan conflict India's dual-capable BrahMos missiles struck a base near Pakistan's nuclear command centres, raising fears of nuclear escalation; Pakistan said it had only 30-45 seconds to judge whether the missile carried a nuclear warhead.

assertions.quote: We did not dissuade the Chinese from undertaking a buildup. They are now in the midst of a buildup.

verdicts.note: US and independent estimates put China's arsenal above 600 warheads and growing toward about 1,000 by 2030, with new silo fields.
A linked Metaculus forecast gives 75% that China has 1,000 nuclear weapons by 2030, consistent with a rapid build-up.

SIPRI estimates China has about 620 warheads and is expanding faster than any other country, with hundreds of missiles loaded into new silo fields; even 1000 by 2030 would be about a quarter of the US or Russian stockpile.

DoD 2025: China's stockpile was in the low 600s through 2024 (production slowed) but the 'massive nuclear expansion' continues and it is on track for over 1,000 warheads by 2030, up from the low 200s in 2020.
US intelligence says China remains intent on modernizing, diversifying and expanding its nuclear posture for rivalry with the US (no warhead count is given here).

assertions.quote: Now we’re in a situation where we’re looking at running simultaneous arms races with the Russians and the Chinese.

verdicts.note: All three are modernizing and China is expanding fast, but US and Russian deployed numbers have not yet grown much past the old treaty limits.

assertions.quote: the Russians are modernising their force to defeat the missile defences the US has and that they fear the US will build.

verdicts.note: Both cite US missile defence to justify new systems, but each also has other motives for its build-up.

US intelligence says Moscow sees US missile defences as a threat to its deterrent and Beijing ties nuclear modernisation to competition with the US, but it gives strategic rivalry as China's driver, not missile defence alone.

RAND describes Russia's Status-6 nuclear drone as a response to US counterforce and missile defences, part of a decades-old 'asymmetric response' strategy; it supports the mechanism for Russia but says nothing here about China's build-up.

The Bulletin says missile defence systems are at best partially effective and serve as a provocation for the other side to invest in greater offensive capability; expert assessment, not a measured response.
Climate models disagree on how much soot burning cities would loft; severe cooling is plausible but its size is disputed.
XPT forecasters judged that in a nuclear exchange nuclear winter is more likely than direct effects to cause a catastrophe, while noting substantial uncertainty in nuclear-winter models.

The introduction, citing Robock et al.'s nuclear-winter modelling, says a war using large fractions of the US and Russian arsenals could severely reduce food production for years; this is background, not the paper's own finding.

assertions.quote: All of them are preparing to resume nuclear testing in case the other ones do.

verdicts.note: All three have expanded test-site activity and Russia revoked its CTBT ratification in 2023, but none has resumed explosive testing on the public record.
The Bulletin says only that the US administration 'may be considering' resuming explosive testing; it reports no Russian or Chinese preparations.

US intelligence reports Russia deratified the Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty and states are 'testing' WMD capabilities, but it reports no preparations by the US, Russia or China for explosive nuclear tests.
